title: Question 4: Election Day Registration

context.text: Placed on the ballot by initiative petition: the Information for Voters labels it a law proposed by initiative petition on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026. The Legislature's Special Joint Committee on Initiative Petitions issued the legislative reports reproduced in the same booklet.

question.text: Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? Election Day Registration: This proposed law would permit eligible individuals to register to vote or update their voter registration address on Election Day. An individual who is eligible to vote could register to vote on Election Day by going to the polling place in the precinct where they live during voting hours and presenting proof of residency and signing a written oath. Proof of residency could be a valid photo identification, or documentation showing the individual’s name and the address where the individual resides, such as a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, residential lease, wireless telephone statement, paycheck, current student fee statement or other document from a post-secondary school, or another government document or correspondence. The written oath would require the individual to certify that they are a citizen of the United States, are at least 18 years old, are not legally prohibited from voting, and have not and will not vote in the same election at another location. The oath would require the individual to acknowledge that providing false information is a felony punishable by not more than 5 years imprisonment or a fine of not more than $10,000, or both. If an individual did not present proof of residency, they would be allowed to cast a provisional ballot, which would be counted only if the individual returned to provide the required information before the close of polls for a municipal election; within two days after a state primary; or within six days after a state election. Individuals who register to vote on Election Day would be registered to vote in future elections as well as in the election taking place that day. Individuals who are already registered to vote would not be able to change their political party affiliation on Election Day. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028.

summary.text: The measure would let eligible individuals register to vote or update their registration address at their polling place on Election Day by presenting proof of residency and signing a written oath; those without proof could cast a provisional ballot. Already-registered voters could not change party affiliation on Election Day. It would take effect January 1, 2028. Statement of fiscal consequences (Executive Office for Administration and Finance): The proposed law has no discernible material fiscal consequences for state and municipal government finances.

measure.yesMeans: A YES VOTE would permit eligible citizens to register to vote or to update their voter registration address at their polling place on Election Day.
measure.noMeans: A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing voter registration.

argumentsFor.text: In the 150-word argument in favor signed by Norma B. Shulman of YES on Election Day Registration, as printed in the Information for Voters: "This law would give eligible Massachusetts citizens the ability to register or update their address on Election Day – an opportunity voters in the rest of New England already have."

argumentsAgainst.text: In the 150-word argument against signed by Amy Carnevale of the Massachusetts Republican Party, as printed in the Information for Voters: "The public welfare demands that elections be protected from fraud. Same-day voter registration prejudices that welfare by eliminating the advance period during which election officials can examine a registrant’s identity, residence, eligibility, or duplicate registration before a ballot is issued."

researchNotes: Ballot text, official yes/no statements and fiscal statements are taken from the Secretary of the Commonwealth's 2026 Information for Voters booklet (PDF text extracted and checked by script). Arguments are quoted from the signed 150-word pro/con statements, which the Commonwealth states reflect the authors' opinions and are not certified as accurate. Both a signed pro and a signed con argument are printed. The booklet's own summary is the Attorney General's; the Secretary's page and Ballotpedia could not be fetched (bot protection), so the ballot list was confirmed from the booklet itself, which covers nine questions.
